nodes.text: means—
a pandemic declaration; or
a declaration of a state of emergency; or
a declaration of a state of disaster.

nodes.heading: Right to privacy and support when reporting

nodes.text: A person making a report under this Part at a police station or a place approved by the Chief Commissioner of Police—
is entitled to make the report out of the hearing of members of the public; and

is entitled to be accompanied by a support person of his or her own choosing and, in the case of a child, must be accompanied by a parent of the child or, if a parent is not available, an independent person.
A police officer or other person receiving the report may arrange for an interpreter to be present when a person is making a report under this Part.

history.raw: S. 24(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.2).

nodes.text: A police officer receiving the report must not allow an interpreter to be present when a person is making a report under this Part unless the interpreter has signed an undertaking not to disclose any information derived from the report unless required or authorised by or under any Act or law to do so.

history.raw: S. 24(3) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.2).

nodes.heading: Receipt of information to be acknowledged

nodes.text: As soon as is practicable after receiving a report under this Part, the police officer or other person receiving the report must acknowledge the making of the report.

history.raw: S. 25(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.2).

nodes.text: The acknowledgement must be in writing, must be given to the person who made the report and must include—
the name and signature of the police officer or other person who received the report; and

history.raw: S. 25(2)(a) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.2).

nodes.text: the date and time when, and the place where, the report was received; and
a copy of the information that was reported.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must ensure that a copy of every acknowledgement is retained.
If a report is required to be made in person, the person making the report must also—

present for inspection the registrable offender's driver licence (if any) or any other form of identification or other document specified by the regulations for the purposes of this section to verify or support details in the report; and
provide a photograph of the registrable offender's head and face of a type suitable for use in an Australian passport; and
if not the registrable offender, present for inspection his or her driver licence (if any) or any other form of identification specified by the regulations for the purposes of this section.
The police officer receiving the report may waive the requirements of subsection (1)(a) or (b) if the police officer—

history.raw: S. 26(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.3(a)).

nodes.text: takes the fingerprints, or a fingerscan, of the registrable offender immediately before or after the report is made and, in the case of a child, does so in the presence of a parent of the child or, if a parent is not available, an independent person; or
is otherwise satisfied as to the registrable offender's identity.
The police officer receiving the report may waive the requirements of subsection (1)(c) if he or she is otherwise satisfied as to the person's identity.

history.raw: S. 26(3) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.3(a)).

nodes.text: The police officer receiving a report may copy any document presented to the police officer for inspection under subsection (1)(a) or (c).

history.raw: S. 26(4) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.3(b)).

nodes.text: If a report is made otherwise than in person, the regulations may specify—
the circumstances in which—
information concerning the identity of the registrable offender and the identity of the person making the report; and
a document verifying or supporting details in the report—
are required; and
the manner in which that information or document is to be provided—
but may not require an original document to be provided.

nodes.heading: Power to take fingerprints or fingerscan

nodes.text: A police officer may take, or may cause to be taken by a police custody officer within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Victoria Police Act 2013, the fingerprints or a fingerscan of a registrable offender if—

history.raw: S. 27(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.4(a)), substituted by No. 25/2017 s. 19(1).

nodes.text: the fingerprints or a fingerscan of the registrable offender are not already held by the Chief Commissioner of Police; or
the registrable offender is reporting under this Part and the police officer is not satisfied as to the identity of the registrable offender.

A police officer may only take, or cause to be taken, the fingerprints or a fingerscan of a child under subsection (1) if the child is accompanied by a parent or, if a parent is not available, an independent person.

A police officer of or above the rank of senior sergeant may serve, or may cause to be served, a notice on a registrable offender referred to in subsection (1) directing the registrable offender to attend at a police station specified in the notice within 28 days after service of the notice to have the fingerprints or a fingerscan of the registrable offender taken.
A notice under subsection (3) must—

state that if the registrable offender fails to comply with the notice, an application for a warrant to arrest the registrable offender may be made without further notice to the registrable offender; and
state that the registrable offender may wish to seek legal advice as to the effect of the notice; and
state the name, rank and telephone number of the police officer serving the notice or causing the notice to be served; and
contain the prescribed information, if any.
A notice under subsection (3) must be served by delivering a true copy of the notice to the registrable offender personally.
Section 464ZFAA(6), (7) and (8) of the Crimes Act 1958 apply to a notice served under subsection (3) as if it were a notice served under that section.
Subject to subsection (8), a police officer may take the fingerprints or a fingerscan under subsection (1) of a registrable offender whose reporting obligations under this Act—
have been suspended under Division 6 of Part 3; or
have been suspended under section 32(1)(b); or
have expired under section 34(1)—
only if a notice under subsection (3) has been served on the registrable offender.

A registrable offender referred to in subsection (7) may refuse to have fingerprints or a fingerscan taken and to attend at a police station in compliance with a notice under subsection (3) if the registrable offender demonstrates to the reasonable satisfaction of the police officer referred to in subsection (3)—

if the registrable offender was a registrable offender on the commencement of the initial period, that the registrable offender has been resident in Victoria for not less than 2 years and 6 months in aggregate during the initial period; or

that the registrable offender has been resident in Victoria for a continuous period of 12 months at any time after the expiry of the initial period and was a registrable offender during the whole of that period of 12 months.

A person serving a notice under subsection (3) on a registrable offender referred to in subsection (7) must inform the registrable offender, in a manner likely to be understood by the offender, of the following matters—
that the offender may refuse to comply with the notice;
the grounds on which the offender may refuse to comply; and
that the offender may wish to seek legal advice as to the effect of the notice.
A police officer referred to in subsection (8) must take into account any information provided by the registrable offender.
Before a registrable offender referred to in subsection (7) has fingerprints or a fingerscan taken, a police officer must, in a manner likely to be understood by the offender—
inform the offender of the grounds on which the offender may refuse to have fingerprints or a fingerscan taken; and
ask the offender whether the offender wishes to refuse.

If a registrable offender does not have a knowledge of the English language that is sufficient to enable the person to understand the matters referred to in subsection (9) or (11), the person informing the offender must arrange for the presence of a competent interpreter and defer the giving of the information until the interpreter is present.
In this section—

nodes.heading: initial period
nodes.text: means the period of 3 years commencing on the day on which section 19 of the Sex Offenders Registration Amendment (Miscellaneous) Act 2017 comes into operation.
A police officer receiving a report made in person under this Part may require the registrable offender—

history.raw: S. 27A(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.5(a)).

nodes.text: to be photographed; and
to expose any part of his or her body on which there are any tattoos or permanent distinguishing marks to enable that part of the body to be photographed—
by the police officer or a person authorised by the police officer.

A police officer cannot, under this section, require a registrable offender to expose his or her genitals, the anal area of his or her buttocks or, in the case of females or transgender people who identify as females, their breasts.

history.raw: S. 27A(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.5(b)).

nodes.heading: Reasonable force may be used to obtain fingerprints

nodes.text: Before attempting to exercise a power under section 27 or 27A, the police officer must inform the registrable offender in language likely to be understood by him or her—
of the purpose for which the power is to be exercised and, in the case of a power under section 27(1)(b), why the police officer is not satisfied as to the registrable offender's identity; and

that if the registrable offender refuses to give his or her fingerprints, or to submit to a fingerscan or to expose part of his or her body (as the case requires), voluntarily, reasonable force may be used; and

history.raw: S. 28(2)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.6(b)).

nodes.text: that the fingerprints, fingerscan or photographs will be retained by the Chief Commissioner of Police.

A police officer, or a person authorised by him or her, may use reasonable force to take the fingerprints or a fingerscan of a registrable offender or to expose a part of the body of a registrable offender that the police officer is authorised under section 27A to ask the registrable offender to expose to enable the taking of photographs of that part of the body if—
the registrable offender refuses to co-operate voluntarily; and
the use of reasonable force is authorised by a police officer in charge of a police station at the time of the request or a police officer of or above the rank of sergeant.
If reasonable force is to be used under section 27 or 27A, a person of the same sex as the registrable offender must, if practicable, be the person who uses the reasonable force.
Any photograph taken under section 27A must be taken—
in a place where no members of the public are present; and
if practicable, by a person of the same sex as the registrable offender.
If practicable, any police officer present in a place while a photograph is being taken under section 27A must be of the same sex as the registrable offender.

A registrable offender who is to be photographed under section 27A is entitled to be accompanied by a support person of his or her own choosing and, in the case of a child, must be accompanied by a parent or, if a parent is not available, an independent person.

nodes.heading: Retention of material for certain purposes

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police may retain for law enforcement, crime prevention or child protection purposes any of the following taken under this Division from, or in relation to, a registrable offender whose reporting period ends on or after the commencement day—
copies of any documents;
any fingerprints or fingerscans;
any photographs.
In this section, commencement day means the day on which section 13 of the Sex Offenders Registration Amendment Act 2014 comes into operation.

nodes.heading: Retention of material when registration exemption order made
nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police may retain for law enforcement, crime prevention or child protection purposes any of the following taken under this Division from, or recorded in relation to, a registrable offender who is made subject to a registration exemption order—
copies of any documents;
fingerprints or fingerscans;
photographs;
a forensic sample taken under section 464ZFAB of the Crimes Act 1958 and any related material and information within the meaning of section 464(2) of that Act.
This section applies if a registrable offender resides more than the prescribed distance from the nearest police station.
A registrable offender need not comply with a time limit concerning the making of a report in person under this Part if—
he or she, or a person entitled to make the report on his or her behalf, contacts the Chief Commissioner of Police before the time limit expires; and
the Chief Commissioner of Police agrees to allow the report to be made at a specific time that is after the time limit and at a specific place; and
before the time limit expires he or she provides the Chief Commissioner of Police by telephone or other means with the information required to be reported under Division 1 or 2.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must ensure that there is a method of recording all agreements made under this section.

nodes.heading: Suspension and extension of reporting obligations
Suspension and extension of reporting obligations

nodes.text: Any obligation imposed on a registrable offender by this Part is suspended for any period during which he or she—
is in government custody; or
is outside Victoria unless he or she is a person to whom Division 9 applies or the obligation is under section 19; or
is the subject of an order under Division 6 (or an equivalent order made under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction); or
is the subject of a notice under section 45A.
The period for which a registrable offender's reporting obligations continue is extended by any length of time for which those obligations are suspended under subsection (1)(a).

history.raw: S. 33 amended by No. 28/2025 s. 26 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Division, a registrable offender's reporting obligations in respect of a registrable offence begin—
when the registrable offender is sentenced for the offence; or
when the registrable offender ceases to be in government custody in relation to the offence—
whichever is the later.

If a registrable offender's reporting period expires, but the registrable offender is then required to report again under section 35AA, the registrable offender's reporting obligations begin on the day on which—
the registrable offender first becomes a registrable offender to whom section 35AA applies; or
the registrable offender ceases to be in government custody—
whichever occurs later.
A registrable offender must continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for—
8 years, if he or she has only ever been found guilty of a single Class 2 offence; or
15 years, if he or she—
has only ever been found guilty of a single Class 1 offence (other than an offence referred to in item 2 or item 4 of Schedule 1); or
has ever been found guilty of 2 Class 2 offences; or
the remainder of his or her life, if he or she—
has ever been found guilty of 2 or more Class 1 offences; or
has ever been found guilty of a single offence referred to in item 2 or item 4 of Schedule 1; or

history.raw: S. 34(1)(c)(ia) inserted by No. 18/2008 s. 18(2), amended by No. 47/2016 s. 43(1)(b).

nodes.text: has ever been found guilty of a Class 1 offence and 1 or more Class 2 offences; or
has ever been found guilty of 3 or more Class 2 offences.

If every registrable offence for which a person has been found guilty is committed when he or she is a child, the reporting period is reduced—see section 35.  If one or more of the offences for which a person has ever been found guilty is committed when that person is an adult, the reporting periods specified in section 34 apply as if the Act did not contain section 35.

history.raw: Note to s. 34(1) substituted by No. 55/2009 s. 45(1).

nodes.text: A life-long reporting obligation may be suspended under Division 6.
A reference in subsection (1) to an offence extends to an offence committed as a child.
A reference in subsection (1) to an offence extends to an offence committed before the commencement of that subsection.
For the purposes of this section—
2 or more offences arising from the same incident are to be treated as a single offence; and
2 or more offences arising from the same incident are to be treated as a single Class 1 offence if at least one of those offences is a Class 1 offence.
The meaning of single offence is qualified by section 5(1).
For the purposes of this Division, a person subject to a sex offender registration order—
if found guilty of a Class 3 offence is deemed to have been found guilty of a Class 1 offence; and
if found guilty of a Class 4 offence or any other offence other than a Class 3 offence is deemed to have been found guilty of a Class 2 offence.

nodes.heading: Reduced period applies for juvenile registrable offenders

nodes.text: The reporting periods specified in section 34 do not apply to a person who was a child at the time at which he or she committed each registrable offence.
Instead, a reporting period that is half the reporting period that would otherwise apply to the person under section 34 (or 7½ years in the case of a reporting period for life) applies to him or her.
This section does not apply if a person has committed a registrable offence as an adult in addition to an offence or offences committed as a child.

nodes.heading: Reporting period for serious sex offender
nodes.text: 2. The term serious sex offence is not related to the term serious sexual offender.
A registrable offender who—
is an eligible offender by reason of a custodial sentence having been imposed on the offender for a serious sex offence; and
is subject to a supervision order or detention order—
must comply with the reporting obligations in Part 3 for the period specified in subsection (2) or
In the case of a registrable offender who is not subject to a sex offender registration order—
for the reporting period specified in section 34 or 35 that applies to the offender; or
for the period ending 5 years after the supervision order or detention order expires—
whichever ends later.
See also sections 21 and 70 of the Serious Offenders Act 2018 for when a supervision order or detention order expires.
In the case of a registrable offender who is subject to a sex offender registration order—
for the reporting period specified in the sex offender registration order; or

if the reporting period specified in the sex offender registration order ends after the expiry of the supervision order or detention order but before the fifth anniversary of the expiry of the supervision order or detention order, for—
the reporting period specified in the sex offender registration order; and
the period—
beginning immediately after that reporting period ends; and
ending on the fifth anniversary of the expiry of the supervision order or detention order; or

if the reporting period specified in the sex offender registration order ends before the expiry of the supervision order or detention order, for the period ending 5 years after the expiry of the supervision order or detention order—
whichever ends later.
See also sections 21 and 70 of the Serious Offenders Act 2018 for when a supervision order or detention order expires.

If a supervision order or detention order expires on the commencement of another supervision order or detention order replacing it, the period in subsection (2) or (3) is to be determined by reference to the expiry of the supervision order or detention order that replaced it.

If a supervision order or detention order expires and another supervision order or detention order is later made in respect of the offender, the period in subsection (2) or (3) is to be determined by reference to the expiry of the later supervision order or detention order.

1. If a supervision order or detention order expires without another supervision order or detention order replacing it or without another supervision order or detention order being later made in respect of the offender, the period in subsection
or (3) is to be determined by reference to the expiry of that supervision order or detention order.

nodes.heading: Reporting period to run during suspension
nodes.text: If the Supreme Court grants a suspension order under section 40(1A) in respect of a registrable offender who is not required to continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for the remainder of his or her life, the period of suspension of the registrable offender's reporting period is counted when calculating the remainder of that reporting period.

nodes.heading: Reporting period to run while registration exemption order in force
nodes.text: If a court makes a registration exemption order in respect of a registrable offender and that order is set aside on appeal, the period during which the registration exemption order was in force is counted when calculating the remainder of the registrable offender's reporting period.

nodes.heading: Extended reporting period if registrable offender still on parole

nodes.text: This section applies if—
a registrable offender is on parole, or is an existing licensee, in respect of a registrable offence; and
the reporting period in respect of the offence will end before the expiry of the sentence of imprisonment to which the parole or existing licence relates.
Despite anything to the contrary in this Division, the reporting period is extended until the expiry of the term of imprisonment to which the parole or existing licence relates.

nodes.heading: Reporting period for corresponding registrable offenders

nodes.text: A corresponding registrable offender must continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part until he or she would not be required, if he or she were in a foreign jurisdiction, to report to the corresponding registrar of that foreign jurisdiction.

For the purposes of this section, if a corresponding registrable offender is a corresponding registrable offender under the laws of more than one jurisdiction, the period for which he or she must continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part is the longest period for which he or she would be required to report to the corresponding registrar of a foreign jurisdiction.

nodes.heading: Reporting period for New South Wales registrable offenders

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (2), a New South Wales registrable offender must continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for the period he or she is required to report in accordance with the New South Wales Act.

A New South Wales registrable offender who, on or after the date specified by the regulations for the purposes of section 10, is sentenced for a registrable offence or becomes a corresponding registrable offender must continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for—
the period referred to in subsection (1); or
the period that he or she is required to report in accordance with this Division (other than this section)—
whichever is longer.

history.raw: Pt 3 Div. 6 (Heading) substituted by No. 82/2014 s. 15(1).

nodes.heading: Supreme Court may suspend certain registrable offenders' reporting obligations

nodes.text: This section applies to a registrable offender who is required to continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for the remainder of his or her life.
If—

a period of 15 years has passed (ignoring any period during which the registrable offender was in government custody) since he or she was last sentenced or released from government custody in respect of a registrable offence or a corresponding registrable offence, whichever is later; and
he or she did not become the subject of a life-long reporting period under a corresponding Act whilst in a foreign jurisdiction before becoming the subject of such a period in Victoria; and
he or she is not on parole in respect of a registrable offence—
the registrable offender may apply to the Supreme Court for an order suspending his or her reporting obligations.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner may apply for suspension from reporting obligations

history.raw: S. 39A inserted by No. 55/2009 s. 35, amended by No. 25/2017 s. 12(1)(2)(ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner may at any time apply to a court for an order suspending the reporting obligations under this Part of a registrable offender.
Subject to this section, an application under subsection (1) must be made—
to the court that imposed the sentence at first instance for the registrable offence committed by the registrable offender; or
if the registrable offender has been sentenced for more than one registrable offence in more than one court, to the court of the highest jurisdiction that imposed a sentence at first instance.
An application under subsection (1) must be made to the Magistrates' Court if the registrable offender—
has been sentenced by the Children's Court for one or more registrable offences; and
has not been sentenced for a registrable offence by any other court; and
is of or over the age of 21 years at the time the application is made.

An application under subsection (1) that relates to a person who is a registrable offender because the person is a corresponding registrable offender or a New South Wales registrable offender or was sentenced for an offence in a foreign jurisdiction must be made to—
the Supreme Court, if the person to whom the application relates is of or over the age of 18 years at the time the application is made; or
the Children's Court, if the person to whom the application relates is a child at the time the application is made.

nodes.heading: How application is made
nodes.text: An application under section 39 or 39A is made by filing with the relevant court referred to in that section a document in writing—
stating the grounds on which the application is made; and
containing the information, if any, prescribed by the rules of court.
On the application under section 39(2), the Supreme Court may make an order suspending the registrable offender's reporting obligations.

On the application under section 39A, a court may make an order suspending the registrable offender's reporting obligations for the period of time specified in the order (which may be the remainder of the offender's life).

history.raw: S. 40(1A) inserted by No. 55/2009 s. 36(1), amended by No. 25/2017 s. 14(1).

nodes.text: A court must not make an order under this section unless it is satisfied that—

history.raw: S. 40(2) amended by No. 55/2009 s. 36(2), substituted by No. 25/2017 s. 14(2).

nodes.text: the registrable offender poses no risk or a low risk to the sexual safety of one or more persons or of the community; and
it is in the public interest to suspend the registrable offender's reporting obligations.
In deciding whether to make an order under this section, a court must take into account—
the seriousness of the registrable offender's registrable offences and corresponding registrable offences; and
the period of time since those offences were committed; and

the age of the registrable offender, the age of the victims of those offences and the difference in age between the registrable offender and the victims of those offences, as at the time those offences were committed; and
the registrable offender's present age; and
the registrable offender's total criminal record; and
any other matter the court considers appropriate.
In deciding whether to make an order under subsection (1), the Supreme Court must also take into account any submissions made by the Chief Commissioner under section 41.

history.raw: S. 40(4) inserted by No. 55/2009 s. 36(4), amended by No. 25/2017 s. 14(4).

nodes.text: In deciding whether to make an order under subsection (1A), a court must also take into account any evidence presented by the Chief Commissioner as to the risk that the registrable offender presents to the sexual safety of one or more persons or the community.

history.raw: S. 40(5) inserted by No. 55/2009 s. 36(4), amended by No. 25/2017 s. 14(5).

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner is party to application
nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police is a party to an application under section 39(2) and may make any submission to the Supreme Court in respect of the application.

nodes.heading: No costs to be awarded
nodes.text: A court may not award costs in respect of proceedings under this Division.

nodes.heading: Restriction on right of unsuccessful applicant to re-apply for order
nodes.text: A registrable offender in respect of whom the Supreme Court refuses to make an order under section 40(1) is not entitled to make a further application to the Court until 5 years have elapsed from the date of the refusal, unless the Court otherwise orders at the time of the refusal.
An order made under this Division ceases to have effect if, at any time after the making of the order, the registrable offender—
is made subject to a sex offender registration order; or
is found guilty of a registrable offence; or
becomes a corresponding registrable offender who must under section 37 continue to comply with the reporting obligations imposed by this Part for any period.
An order that ceased to have effect in accordance with subsection (1) is revived if—
the finding of guilt that caused the order to cease to have effect is quashed or set aside by a court; or

the order ceased to have effect in accordance with subsection (1)(a) and the sex offender registration order is quashed on appeal or the registrable offender's finding of guilt in respect of the offence that resulted in the making of that order is quashed or set aside by a court.
For the purposes of this section, it is irrelevant whether or not a person may lodge, or has lodged, an appeal in respect of a finding of guilt or a sex offender registration order.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner may apply for revocation of suspension order

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner may apply to a court for the revocation of an order made by that court under section 40(1A) on the ground that the circumstances in which that order was sought have materially changed.
The order under section 40(1A) ceases to have effect on the making of an order under subsection (1).
If an order ceases to have effect in accordance with section 44(1), the registrable offender may apply under this Division for a new order.
If an order ceases to have effect in accordance with section 44(1), the Chief Commissioner may apply under this Division for a new order.
Section 43 does not apply with respect to an application referred to in subsection (1).

If an order ceases to have effect in accordance with section 44(1)(b) or (c), on an application under section 39(2) for a new order, section 39(2)(a) applies as if the period referred to were a period of 15 years (ignoring any period during which he or she was in government custody) since he or she last committed a registrable offence or a corresponding registrable offence.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner of Police may suspend reporting obligations for period not exceeding

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (2), the Chief Commissioner of Police, by written notice served on a registrable offender, may suspend the registrable offender's reporting obligations for a period (not exceeding 5 years) specified in the notice.

The Chief Commissioner of Police must not act under subsection (1) unless satisfied that the registrable offender does not pose a risk or poses a low risk to the sexual safety of one or more persons or of the community.
In deciding whether to act under subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police must take into account—
the seriousness of the registrable offender's registrable offences and corresponding registrable offences; and
the period of time since those offences were committed; and

the age of the registrable offender, the age of the victims of those offences and the difference in age between the registrable offender and the victims of those offences, as at the time those offences were committed; and
the registrable offender's present age; and
the registrable offender's total criminal record; and
the extent to which the registrable offender has complied with their reporting obligations; and
the registrable offender's physical or cognitive capacity to comply with their reporting obligations; and
any other matter that the Chief Commissioner of Police considers appropriate.
The Chief Commissioner of Police—
may suspend a registrable offender's reporting obligations more than once; and
may cancel a suspension under this section at any time.
A suspension under this section is taken to be cancelled if during the period of the suspension an order is made under section 40 in respect of the registrable offender.

nodes.heading: Offence of failing to comply with reporting obligations

nodes.text: A registrable offender who without reasonable excuse fails to comply with any of the registrable offender's reporting obligations (other than reporting obligations in respect of details to which section 14 applies) is guilty of an offence and liable to level 6 imprisonment (5 years maximum).

history.raw: S. 46(1) amended by No. 52/2007 s. 16, substituted by No. 82/2014 s. 17.

nodes.text: A registrable offender who without reasonable excuse fails to comply with any of the registrable offender's reporting obligations in respect of details to which section 14(1)(d), (da), (db), (dc), (dd), (e), (ea), (f), (g), (j), (k) or (m) applies is guilty of an offence and liable to level 6 imprisonment (5 years maximum).

A registrable offender who without reasonable excuse fails to comply with any of the registrable offender's reporting obligations in respect of details to which section 14(1)(a), (b), (c), (h), (i) or (l) applies is guilty of an offence and liable to level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum).

In determining whether a person had a reasonable excuse for failing to comply with his or her reporting obligations, the court before which the proceedings are being heard is to have regard to the following matters—
the person's age; and
whether the person has a disability that affects the person's ability to understand, or to comply with, those obligations; and

whether the form of notification given to the registrable offender as to his or her obligations was adequate to inform him or her of those obligations, having regard to the offender's circumstances; and
any other matter the court considers appropriate.

It is a defence to proceedings for an offence of failing to comply with a reporting obligation if it is established by or on behalf of the person charged with the offence that, at the time the offence is alleged to have occurred, the person had not received notice, and was otherwise unaware, of the obligation.

nodes.heading: Offence of furnishing false or misleading information

nodes.text: A registrable offender who in purported compliance with this Part furnishes details (other than details to which section 14 applies) that the registrable offender knows to be false or misleading in a material particular is guilty of an offence and liable to level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum) or a level 7 fine (240 penalty units).

A registrable offender who in purported compliance with this Part furnishes details to which section 14(1)(d), (da), (db), (dc), (dd), (e), (ea), (f), (g), (j), (k) or (m) applies that the registrable offender knows to be false or misleading in a material particular is guilty of an offence and liable to level 6 imprisonment (5 years maximum).

A registrable offender who in purported compliance with this Part furnishes details to which section 14(1)(a), (b), (c), (h), (i) or (l) applies that the registrable offender knows to be false or misleading in a material particular is guilty of an offence and liable to level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum).

A police officer of or above the rank of senior sergeant may apply to a magistrate for the issue of a search warrant in relation to particular premises or a place (including a vehicle in or on the premises or the place) if the police officer suspects on reasonable grounds that—
an offence against this Act has been, is being or is likely to be committed; and
it is necessary to search the particular premises or the place (including a vehicle in or on the premises or the place) in order—
to investigate or prevent the commission of that offence or the continuation of the commission of that offence; or
to enable evidentiary material to be obtained of the commission of that offence or of the identity or location of an offender.
In addition to any other requirement, an application for a search warrant under this section must state—
the name and rank of the applicant; and
the particulars of the grounds on which the application is based; and
the address or other description of the premises or place to be searched; and
if the warrant is sought to search for a particular thing, a full description of that thing and, if known, its location; and
if the warrant is sought to search for a particular kind of thing, a description of the kind of thing; and
if a previous application for the same warrant was refused, details of the refusal; and
any other prescribed information.

On an application under subsection (1), if a magistrate is satisfied by evidence on oath, whether oral or by affidavit, that there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that an offence against this Act has been, is being or is about to be committed, and that it is necessary to search the particular premises or a place (including a vehicle in or on the premises or the place) for a purpose specified in subsection (1)(b), the magistrate may issue a search warrant authorising the police officer named in the warrant and any assistants the police officer considers necessary—
to enter the particular premises or place or vehicle named or described in the warrant; and
to search for and seize any evidence of the offence named or described in the warrant, including evidence of the identity or location of an offender.
A search warrant must be issued in accordance with the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 and in the prescribed form under that Act.
The rules to be observed with respect to search warrants set out by or under the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 extend and apply to warrants under this section.
In this section—

nodes.heading: vehicle
nodes.text: includes motor vehicle, aircraft and vessel.

nodes.heading: Expiry of search warrant
nodes.text: A search warrant issued under section 47A ceases to have effect on the earliest of the following—
on the expiry date specified in the warrant;
if no expiry date is specified, at the end of the period of one month after its issue;
when it is executed.

nodes.heading: Power to require assistance from person with knowledge of a computer or computer network
nodes.text: If a magistrate issues a warrant under section 47A, section 465AA (other than subsection (10A)) of the Crimes Act 1958 applies as if—
a reference to the Magistrates' Court were a reference to a magistrate; and
a reference to a warrant under section 465 of the Crimes Act 1958 were a reference to a warrant under section 47A; and
a reference to warrant premises were a reference to the particular premises or place (including a vehicle in or on the premises or place) specified in a warrant issued under section 47A; and
a reference to an indictable offence were a reference to an offence against this Act.

nodes.heading: Time limit for prosecutions waived
nodes.text: Despite anything to the contrary in section 7(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009, a proceeding for an offence under this Act may be commenced at any time.

history.raw: S. 48 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 112.3).

nodes.heading: Bar to prosecution for failing to report leaving Victoria

nodes.text: This section applies if a registrable offender leaves Victoria and is found guilty of failing to report his or her presence in a foreign jurisdiction as required by a corresponding Act.
The registrable offender is not to be prosecuted for a failure to comply with section 18 in respect of the travel out of Victoria.

nodes.heading: Notice to be given to registrable offender

nodes.text: A registrable offender is to be given written notice of—
his or her reporting obligations; and
the consequences that may arise if he or she fails to comply with those obligations.
A notice under subsection (1) must include the details (if any) prescribed by the regulations.
A registrable offender is to be given a notice under this section as soon as practicable after any of the following events happens—
he or she is sentenced for a registrable offence;
he or she is released from government custody (whether in government custody for a registrable offence or not);
he or she enters Victoria if he or she has not previously been given notice of his or her reporting obligations in Victoria;
he or she becomes a corresponding registrable offender, if he or she is in Victoria at that time.
A notice under this section is to be given by the person or body specified in, or determined in accordance with, the regulations.
A person or body is not required to give a notice under this section if the notice has been given by another person or body.
Despite anything in this Division, a court that—
makes any order or imposes any sentence that has the effect of making a person a registrable offender for the purposes of this Act; or
imposes any sentence on a person in relation to a registrable offence—

must ensure that the person is, at the time the order is made or the sentence imposed, given a written notice specifying the reporting period that applies to him or her consequent on the order or sentence.
The court may issue a further notice to correct an error in a notice given to a person under this section.
In subsections (5) and (5A), court does not include a court of a foreign jurisdiction.

history.raw: S. 50(6) inserted by No. 34/2005 s. 17, amended by No. 21/2016 s. 18(2).

nodes.heading: Courts to provide information to Chief Commissioner of Police

nodes.text: This section applies if a court—
makes any order or imposes any sentence that has the effect of making a person a registrable offender for the purposes of this Act; or
imposes any sentence on a person in relation to a registrable offence; or

determines an appeal made to it by a registrable offender against the finding of guilt or sentence in respect of a registrable offence or against the making of a sex offender registration order in respect of an offence; or

makes any order in relation to a registrable offender that has the effect of removing the person from the ambit of this Act. Example: Paragraph (c) would apply, for instance, if a court on appeal quashes a person's finding of guilt in relation to a registrable offence in respect of which he or she had been sentenced and that was the only offence in respect of which he or she had ever been found guilty.

The court must ensure that details of the order, sentence or determination of appeal are provided to the Chief Commissioner of Police as soon as is practicable after the making or imposition of the order or sentence or the determination of the appeal (as the case requires).
In this section, court does not include a court of a foreign jurisdiction.

nodes.heading: Notice to be given when reporting period changes

nodes.text: This section applies to a registrable offender whose reporting period has changed since he or she was last notified of his or her reporting period in Victoria.

The Chief Commissioner of Police must give (or cause to be given) written notice to the registrable offender as soon as is practicable after the change and in no case later than the time the offender next reports in accordance with this Act.

nodes.heading: Supervising authority to notify Chief Commissioner of Police of certain events

nodes.text: This section applies if a registrable offender—
ceases to be in government custody; or
ceases to be subject to a supervised sentence; or
ceases to participate in a diversion program under section 59 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009; or

history.raw: S. 53(1)(d) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 112.4).

nodes.text: ceases to be subject to a condition of parole requiring the person to be subject to supervision; or
ceases to be an existing licensee—
regardless of the reason why the registrable offender was in custody, was subject to the sentence, was in the program, was on parole or was a licensee.
As soon as is practicable before or after the relevant event listed in subsection (1) occurs, the supervising authority is to give written notice of the event to the Chief Commissioner of Police.
The notice must include any details required by the regulations.

nodes.heading: Notices may be given by Chief Commissioner

history.raw: S. 54 amended by No. 25/2017 s. 32 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police may, at any time, cause written notice to be given to a registrable offender of—
his or her reporting obligations; and
the consequences that may arise if he or she fails to comply with those obligations.
A notice under subsection (1) must include the details (if any) prescribed by the regulations.

nodes.heading: Failure to comply with procedural requirements does not affect registrable offender's obligations
nodes.text: A failure by any person other than a registrable offender to comply with any procedural requirement imposed on the person by this Part or the regulations does not, of itself, affect a registrable offender's reporting obligations.

This section aims to prevent a registrable offender who was not given notice of a reporting obligation by an official as required by this Part from arguing that the obligation does not apply to him or her as a result of that failure if there is evidence that the registrable offender was aware of the obligation through some other means.  (If there is no such evidence then the registrable offender would have a defence to the charge under section 46(3) on the basis that he or she was not aware of the obligation.)

nodes.heading: Modified reporting procedures for protected witnesses

nodes.text: This Division applies to each of the following—
any registrable offender who is currently a participant in a Victorian witness protection program;
any registrable offender who is the subject of an order in force under this Division declaring that he or she is a person to whom this Division applies.

This Division (except sections 58 to 60) also applies to a registrable offender who is receiving protection under a foreign witness protection law specified by the regulations for the purposes of this subsection, or who has the same status as such a person under an order made under a corresponding Act specified by the regulations for the purposes of this subsection.
In this Division, Victorian witness protection program has the same meaning as it has in the Witness Protection Act 1991.

Section 6(5) excludes from the definition of registrable offender persons receiving protection under foreign witness protection laws prescribed for the purposes of that section or who have the same status as such persons under a corresponding Act that is so prescribed.

nodes.heading: Report need not be made in person
nodes.text: It is sufficient compliance with the requirements of this Part—

if a person to whom this Division applies reports such of the information that he or she is required to report under this Part as the Chief Commissioner of Police requires him or her to report and does so at the times, and in a manner, authorised by the Chief Commissioner of Police for the purposes of this section; and
if the acknowledgement of the making of a report is given in a manner approved by the Chief Commissioner of Police.

nodes.heading: Order as to whether this Division applies

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police must make an order declaring that a registrable offender who is a participant in a Victorian witness protection program either is, or is not, a person to whom this Division applies—
when the registrable offender ceases to be a participant in the program as a consequence of a request under section 16(1) of the Witness Protection Act 1991; or

when the Chief Commissioner of Police makes a decision under section 16(2) of the Witness Protection Act 1991 that the protection and assistance provided to the registrable offender under the program be terminated.
On making such an order, the Chief Commissioner of Police must take reasonable steps to notify the registrable offender of the terms of the order.
A person who receives such a notification may, within 28 days after receiving it, apply in writing to the Chief Commissioner of Police for a review of the order.
On receiving an application for a review, the Chief Commissioner of Police—
must review the order, and confirm or reverse it; and
before making a decision on the matter, must give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to state his or her case; and
after making a decision on the matter, must give written notice of the decision to the applicant.
If the decision of the Chief Commissioner of Police is to confirm the order, the notice of the decision must inform the applicant of his or her rights under section 59.

A person who is aggrieved by a decision of the Chief Commissioner of Police in relation to an order under this Division may appeal to the IBAC against the decision within 3 days after receiving notice of the decision.
The IBAC, in determining the appeal, may make any decision that could have been made by the Chief Commissioner of Police.
The IBAC's decision in respect of the appeal has effect according to its terms.
An order declaring that this Division applies to a registrable offender takes effect immediately.
An order declaring that this Division does not apply to a registrable offender takes effect—
at the end of 28 days after notice of the making of the order is given to the registrable offender; or
if an application referred to in section 58(3) is made before the end of that period, at the end of 3 days after notice is given to the applicant as referred to in section 58(4)(c); or
if an appeal is made under section 59 before the end of that 3 day period, on the date on which the IBAC determines the appeal—
whichever is the later.

nodes.heading: Modification of ongoing reporting obligations
nodes.text: Sections 14(1), 18 to 21A and 49 apply with respect to a person to whom this Division applies as if any reference in them to Victoria were a reference to the jurisdiction in which the person generally resides.

nodes.heading: Publication of information about registrable offender who fails to comply with reporting obligations

history.raw: Pt 3 Div. 10 (Heading and ss 61A–61G) inserted by No. 21/2016 s. 11.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner of Police may publish information if registrable offender cannot be located

nodes.text: Subject to sections 61B and 61C, the Chief Commissioner of Police may publish, on an Internet site maintained by the Chief Commissioner, information about a registrable offender if—
the Chief Commissioner is satisfied that the registrable offender—
has failed to comply with the registrable offender's reporting obligations; or
in purported compliance with the registrable offender's reporting obligations, has reported details that are false or misleading in any particular; and
the Chief Commissioner is satisfied that publishing the information may—
assist police in locating the registrable offender; or
protect the sexual safety of the community; and
the registrable offender's whereabouts are not known to the Chief Commissioner.
The Chief Commissioner of Police may publish under subsection (1)—
personal information about a registrable offender, including—
any photographs of the registrable offender; and
subject to section 61C(4), information reported by the registrable offender under this Part; and
information disclosing that the registrable offender is a registrable offender.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner of Police must attempt to notify registrable offender before publication
nodes.text: If the Chief Commissioner of Police intends to publish information under section 61A(1) about a registrable offender, the Chief Commissioner must make reasonable efforts to contact the registrable offender and advise that information about the registrable offender may be published if the offender does not report to the Chief Commissioner.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must not publish under section 61A—
any information about a registrable offender who is a child; or
any information that may identify a child (including a registrable offender who is a child).
The Chief Commissioner of Police must not publish under section 61A any information about a registrable offender to whom Division 9 applies.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must consult with the Commissioner for Corrections before publishing under section 61A any information about a registrable offender who is—
on parole; or
subject to a supervision order, an interim supervision order, a detention order, an interim detention order or an emergency detention order within the meaning of the Serious Offenders Act 2018.

The Chief Commissioner of Police must not publish under section 61A any personal details reported by the registrable offender under section 14(1)(d), (f) or (g) unless any other person to whom those details relate (or the other person's representative) has been notified of the intended publication.
Despite subsection (4), the Chief Commissioner of Police is not required to notify a person if the notification would compromise a police investigation.

nodes.heading: Chief Commissioner of Police to take into account certain matters before publishing
nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police may have regard to any of the following in deciding whether to publish information about a registrable offender under section 61A—
the benefit to the community of publication;
the effect that publication might have on a victim of an offence committed by the registrable offender;
if known, the views of a victim of an offence committed by the registrable offender;
any medical, psychiatric, psychological or other assessment relating to the registrable offender;
any information indicating whether or not the registrable offender is likely to commit an offence in future;
whether or not there is a pattern of offending behaviour on the part of the registrable offender;
the registrable offender's criminal record;
if the registrable offender is awaiting trial for an offence, whether the publication might prejudice the fair trial of the registrable offender;
any other matter that the Chief Commissioner of Police considers relevant.

As soon as practicable after the registrable offender about whom information was published is located (whether or not by making a report to police), the Chief Commissioner of Police must remove from the Internet site any information about the registrable offender published under section 61A(1).
In addition to subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police may, at any time, remove from the Internet site any information published under section 61A(1).
The Chief Commissioner of Police may, at any time, republish, in accordance with section 61A, any information removed under this section.

nodes.heading: Disclosure by senior police of personal information published under this Division
nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police or a police officer of or above the rank of superintendent may disclose personal information about a registrable offender if that information—
has been published by the Chief Commissioner of Police under section 61A(1); and
at the time of making the disclosure, has not been removed from the Internet site by the Chief Commissioner of Police under section 61E.

nodes.heading: Offence—republication by third parties that would incite, or would be likely to incite, animosity or harassment

nodes.text: This section applies in respect of information about a registrable offender that has been published by the Chief Commissioner of Police under section 61A(1).

A person must not publish information about a registrable offender if the person knows, or ought reasonably to know, that the publication would create, promote or increase animosity towards, or harassment of, the registrable offender or an associate of the registrable offender.
Penalty: In the case of an individual, 240 penalty units or 2 years imprisonment; In the case of a body corporate, 1200 penalty units.
The Chief Commissioner of Police is to establish and maintain, or arrange for another entity to establish and maintain, a Register of Sex Offenders.
The Register is to contain the following information in respect of each registrable offender (to the extent that it is known by the Chief Commissioner of Police)—
the registrable offender's name and other identifying particulars; and
details of each Class 1 or Class 2 offence of which the registrable offender has been found guilty or with which he or she has been charged; and
details of each offence of which the registrable offender has been found guilty that resulted in the making of a sex offender registration order; and
the date on which the registrable offender was sentenced for any registrable offence; and

the date on which the registrable offender ceased to be in government custody in respect of a registrable offence, or entered or ceased to be in government custody in respect of any offence during his or her reporting period; and
any information reported in respect of the registrable offender under Part 3; and
if a prohibition order or a registration order has been made against the registrable offender, the details of that order; and
any other information that the Chief Commissioner of Police considers appropriate to include in the Register.

nodes.heading: Access to the Register to be restricted

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police must ensure—
that the Register, or any part of the Register, is only accessed by a person, or a class of person, who is authorised to do so by the Chief Commissioner of Police; and
that personal information in the Register is only disclosed in accordance with this Act.

history.raw: S. 63(1)(b) amended by No. 34/2005 s. 20(1)(a)–(c), substituted by No. 52/2007 s. 17.

nodes.text: Despite subsection (1)(b), the Chief Commissioner of Police may notify the Registrar within the meaning of the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1996 of the name (including any other name by which he or she is, or has previously been, known), date of birth and residential address or addresses of any registrable offender as stated in the Register.

Despite subsection (1)(b), for the purposes of administering the Worker Screening Act 2020, the Chief Commissioner of Police may notify the Regulator within the meaning of that Act of the name (including any other name by which he or she is, or has previously been, known), date of birth and residential address or addresses of any registrable offender as stated in the Register.

history.raw: S. 63(1B) inserted by No. 55/2009 s. 47, amended by Nos 34/2020 s. 241, 58/2025 s. 125(Sch. 2 item 5).

nodes.text: Despite subsection (1)(b), for the purposes of administering the Firearms Act 1996, the Chief Commissioner of Police may notify the Firearms Appeals Committee established under Part 9 of that Act, and any person assisting that Committee, of part or all of the information relating to a registrable offender that is in the Register.

The Chief Commissioner of Police must develop guidelines in relation to the accessing and disclosure of personal information in the Register that support access and disclosure of personal information in the Register occurring only to the extent authorised or permitted in accordance with this Act.

For the purposes of this section, the Register includes any information from any register maintained under a corresponding Act that is accessible by the Chief Commissioner of Police, regardless of whether or not that information is physically part of the Register.
This section has effect despite any other Act or law to the contrary.

nodes.heading: Person with access to Register not to disclose personal information from it

nodes.text: A person authorised to have access to the Register or any part of the Register must not disclose any personal information in the Register to any person.
Penalty: 240 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years.

Despite subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police or a person authorised to have access to the Register or any part of the Register may disclose personal information in the Register to a government department, public statutory authority or court—
for the purpose of judicial functions or activities; or
for the purpose of the performance of a function of a law enforcement agency under any Act or law; or
as authorised or required by or under any Act or law; or
if the Chief Commissioner or a person authorised to have access to the Register believes on reasonable grounds that to do so is necessary to enable the proper administration of this Act; or
for the purposes of an order made under Part 4A (other than an order under section 66ZD or 66ZE).

Despite subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police or a person authorised to have access to the Register or any part of the Register may disclose personal information in the Register to the Australian Crime Commission for entry on the Australian National Child Offender Register.

history.raw: S. 64(3) inserted by No. 20/2015 s. 15, amended by No. 54/2016 s. 38(1).

nodes.text: Despite subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police or a person authorised to have access to the Register or any part of the Register may disclose personal information from the Register as authorised by Division 10 of Part 3.
Despite subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose personal information from the Register as authorised by section 66ZZC.
Despite subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose personal information in the Register as authorised by Part 5D.
In this section—

nodes.text: Victoria Police; or
the police force or police service (however described) of a foreign jurisdiction;

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police, if the Chief Commissioner considers it appropriate to do so, may provide to any person information in the Register in respect of one or more registrable offenders if the information is de-identified information.
The Chief Commissioner of Police may impose any restriction or condition that the Chief Commissioner thinks fit on the use of de-identified information disclosed under subsection (1).
A person to whom de-identified information is disclosed under subsection (1) must comply with any restriction or condition on its use that is imposed by the Chief Commissioner.
Penalty: 10 penalty units in the case of a natural person; 50 penalty units in the case of a body corporate.
In this section—

nodes.heading: de-identified information
nodes.text: means information about an individual whose identity, or the identity of any other individual, is not apparent or cannot reasonably be ascertained from the information.

nodes.heading: Restriction on who may access personal information on protected witnesses
nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police must ensure that any personal information in the Register about a person to whom Division 9 of Part 3 applies cannot be accessed other than by a person authorised by the police officer or officer of an approved authority (within the meaning of the Witness Protection Act 1991) responsible for the day to day operation of the witness protection program.

history.raw: S. 65 amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.7).

nodes.heading: Registrable offender's rights in relation to Register

nodes.text: If asked to do so by a registrable offender, the Chief Commissioner of Police must provide the registrable offender with a copy of all the reportable information that is held in the Register in relation to the registrable offender.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must comply with subsection (1) as soon as is practicable after being asked to do so.
A registrable offender may ask the Chief Commissioner of Police to amend any reportable information held in the Register in relation to the registrable offender that is incorrect.
The Chief Commissioner of Police must comply with such a request on being satisfied that the information is incorrect.

In this section, reportable information means any information supplied to the Chief Commissioner of Police by, or on behalf of, the registrable offender that the registrable offender is required to report to the Chief Commissioner and that is still held in the Register.

nodes.heading: Sexual safety of the community paramount in prohibition order decisions

nodes.text: The court must give paramount consideration to the sexual safety of the community in deciding whether to—
make, vary, revoke or extend a prohibition order; or
vary a corresponding prohibition order before registration or vary a registration order.

For the purposes of subsection (1), it is not necessary that the court be able to identify a risk posed by the registrable offender to the sexual safety of a particular person or a particular class of person.

nodes.heading: When is a registrable offender properly notified of an order?

history.raw: S. 66C inserted by No. 79/2004 s. 101 (as amended by No. 97/2004 s. 9(7)), amended by Nos 34/2008 s. 143(Sch. 2 items 10.2, 10.3), 82/2012 s. 134, 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 154.9), repealed by No. 21/2016 s. 14.

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, a registrable offender is properly notified of an order—
if the registrable offender is before the court when the order is made, on the making of the order; or
otherwise, when a copy of the order is served on the registrable offender.

An order made under this Part has effect on its making but a prohibition order or a registration order, or an order varying a prohibition order or a variation order, cannot be enforced against a registrable offender until the registrable offender is properly notified that the order has been made.

New s. 66D inserted by No. 21/2016 s. 8.

nodes.text: The Chief Commissioner of Police may apply for a prohibition order in respect of a registrable offender.
An application under subsection (1) must be made—
if the registrable offender is a child, to the Criminal Division of the Children's Court; or
in any other case, to the Magistrates' Court.
An application under subsection (1) must—
be made in writing; and
include the name of the registrable offender; and
include an affidavit made by a police officer setting out the grounds on which the prohibition order is sought; and
include any other information prescribed by the regulations.
An application for a prohibition order must be served on the registrable offender as soon as practicable after the application is made.

nodes.heading: Court may make an interim prohibition order

nodes.text: The court may make an interim prohibition order on an application under section 66D if the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that—
the registrable offender poses a risk to the sexual safety of one or more persons or of children or the community generally; and
it is necessary to make an interim prohibition order to reduce that risk pending a final decision about the application.
If the registrable offender is an adult, the court may make an interim prohibition order—
whether or not the registrable offender has been served with a copy of the application for the prohibition order; and
whether or not the registrable offender is present when the interim prohibition order is made.
If the registrable offender is an adult, the court may make an interim prohibition order by consent of the parties—
without being satisfied as to any matter in subsection (1); and
without conducting a hearing in relation to the particulars of the application unless, in the court's opinion, it is in the interests of justice to do so.
For the purposes of subsection (3)(b), in determining whether it is in the interests of justice to conduct a hearing, the court may take into account whether the registrable offender—
is legally represented; or
has impaired intellectual functioning; or
is a person in respect of whom a guardianship order is in force; or
has the capacity to understand the proceeding; or
may otherwise be prevented from understanding the effect of consenting to the order.
If the court makes an interim prohibition order, the court must give the registrable offender a written notice that—
states that the interim prohibition order has been made; and
states that it is an offence to contravene the interim prohibition order, and the maximum penalties that apply to a contravention; and
includes any other prescribed information.
The written notice must—
if the registrable offender is before the court, be given to the registrable offender with the copy of the interim prohibition order; or
if the registrable offender is not before the court, be served on the registrable offender with the copy of the interim prohibition order.

nodes.heading: Hearing to be listed about final prohibition order as soon as practicable
nodes.text: If the court makes an interim prohibition order, the court must ensure the application under section 66D is listed for hearing about the final prohibition order as soon as practicable.

nodes.heading: Duration of interim prohibition orders
nodes.text: An interim prohibition order ends on the earliest of the following—
if the interim prohibition order is revoked by the court, on its revocation;
if the court makes a final prohibition order, when the registrable offender is properly notified of the making of the final prohibition order;
if the court refuses to make a final prohibition order, on the refusal to make the order;
if the application under section 66D is withdrawn, at the time the application is withdrawn.

nodes.heading: Court may make a final prohibition order

nodes.text: The court may make a final prohibition order if the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that—
the registrable offender has engaged in behaviour alleged in the application; and
having regard to the nature and pattern of that behaviour, that the registrable offender poses a risk to the sexual safety of one or more persons or of children or the community generally; and
making the final prohibition order will reduce that risk.

For the purposes of subsection (1)(b), it is not necessary that the court be able to identify a risk posed by the registrable offender to the sexual safety of a particular person or a particular class of person.
If the registrable offender is an adult, the court may make a final prohibition order by consent of the parties—
without being satisfied as to any matter in subsection (1); and
without conducting a hearing in relation to the particulars of the application unless, in the court's opinion, it is in the interests of justice to do so.
For the purposes of subsection (3)(b), in determining whether it is in the interests of justice to conduct a hearing, the court may take into account whether the registrable offender—
is legally represented; or
has impaired intellectual functioning; or
is a person in respect of whom a guardianship order is in force; or
has the capacity to understand the proceeding; or
may otherwise be prevented from understanding the effect of consenting to the order.

nodes.heading: Considerations in making a final prohibition order
nodes.text: In determining whether to make a final prohibition order, the court must consider the following—
the registrable offender's findings of guilt or charges for sexual and other relevant offences, and for each offence—
the seriousness and nature of the offence; and
the period since the offence was committed; and
the ages of the registrable offender and the victim of the offence when the offence was committed; and
if the victim was a child when the offence was committed, the age difference between the registrable offender and the victim;
the registrable offender's age;
if known, whether the registrable offender's behaviour alleged in the application is similar to behaviour that was preparatory to previous relevant offences;
the registrable offender's circumstances, to the extent that they relate to the conduct sought to be prohibited by the order;
1 The registrable offender's accommodation and employment needs. 2 The registrable offender's need for reintegration into the community.
whether making the order is proportionate to the risk of the registrable offender committing further registrable offences;
the impact of the conditions of the order on the treatment and rehabilitation of the registrable offender;
the impact of the conditions of the order on the registrable offender's family;
any other matter the court considers relevant.

nodes.heading: Additional considerations if the registrable offender is a child

nodes.text: In addition to the matters in section 66J, in determining whether to make a final prohibition order against a registrable offender who is a child, the Children's Court must consider the following—
the child's educational, training and employment needs;
whether the order would prevent the child accessing therapeutic services, and if so, the availability of alternative strategies to manage the child's behaviour;
the need to strengthen and preserve the relationship between the child and the child's family;
the need to minimise the stigma to the child resulting from the making of a final prohibition order;
the desirability of allowing the child's living arrangements to continue without interruption or disturbance;
if relevant, the need to ensure that the child is aware that the child must bear responsibility for the child's actions against the law.
In addition to the matters specified in subsection
, the Children's Court must have regard to the assessment report, and any community treatment report.

nodes.heading: Children's Court must order assessment report

nodes.text: In determining an application for a final prohibition order against a registrable offender who is a child, the Children's Court must order that an assessment report be prepared by—
the Children's Court Clinic; or
another person or body who has relevant expertise.
An assessment report must include information and assessments about the registrable offender, the registrable offender's family and any other matters stated in the order under subsection (1).

An assessment report must include an opinion about the impact that making the final prohibition order may have on the registrable offender's accommodation, educational, health, cultural and social needs.
The assessment report must be filed with the court within the period specified in the order under subsection (1).
Subject to subsection (6), the Children's Court must release a copy of the assessment report to each party to the proceeding.

The Children's Court, after having regard to the views of the parties to the proceeding, may refuse to release an assessment report or a particular part of an assessment report if the Court is satisfied that the release of the report or part of the report may be prejudicial to the development or mental health of the child.

nodes.heading: Where assessment report raises concerns about impact of final prohibition order

nodes.text: This section applies if—
the Children's Court is satisfied that there are grounds for making a final prohibition order against a registrable offender who is a child; and
the assessment report raises concerns about the impact on the child of making a final prohibition order.
The Children's Court may request the Secretary to the Department of Justice and Community Safety to provide a report to the Court about options for treatment of the child in the community.

nodes.heading: Court to consider interim prohibition order if hearing adjourned
nodes.text: If the hearing of an application for a final prohibition order is adjourned, the court must consider making an interim prohibition order.
If the court makes a final prohibition order, the court must give the registrable offender a written notice that—
states that the final prohibition order has been made; and
states that it is an offence to contravene the final prohibition order, and the maximum penalties that apply to a contravention; and
includes any other prescribed information.
The written notice must—
if the registrable offender is before the court, be given to the registrable offender with the copy of the final prohibition order; or
if the registrable offender is not before the court, be served on the registrable offender with the copy of the final prohibition order.
A final prohibition order remains in force for the period specified by the court, unless it is extended under section 66ZN.
The court must not specify a period that—
if the registrable offender is an adult, is more than 5 years; or
if the registrable offender is a child, is more than 2 years; or
in any case, would exceed the registrable offender's reporting period.

nodes.heading: Conditions to be included in prohibition order

nodes.text: The court may include in a prohibition order any conditions that appear to be necessary or desirable in the circumstances.
Without limiting subsection (1), a prohibition order may include conditions—
prohibiting the registrable offender associating with or otherwise contacting a specified person or class of person; and
Persons aged less than 18 years, victims of the registrable offender or the victim's family members.
prohibiting the registrable offender being in, or anywhere within a specified distance of, a specified place or class of place; and
subject to section 66R, excluding the registrable offender from premises at which the registrable offender generally resides; and
prohibiting the registrable offender from engaging in specified behaviour; and
prohibiting the registrable offender from engaging in specified community activities; and
subject to subsection (3), prohibiting the registrable offender from engaging in specified employment or a specified kind of employment; and
prohibiting the registrable offender from consuming alcohol; and
prohibiting the registrable offender from using, or unlawfully obtaining, a drug of dependence.

In deciding whether to include a condition referred to in subsection (2)(f) in a prohibition order against a registrable offender who is a child, the Children's Court must consider the desirability of allowing the treatment, education, training or employment of the child to continue without interruption or disturbance.
For the purposes of this section and section 66R, employment means—
work carried out under a contract of employment; or
work carried out as a self-employed person or as a sub-contractor; or
work carried out as a volunteer for an organisation; or
